Why the Powerball jackpot looks small

It isn’t a mistake. After the $847 million jackpot was won in New Jersey on November 4, Powerball rebuilt to $114 million — and that prize was won on Saturday, November 21, so the jackpot has reset again to its $20 million starting level for Monday’s draw. Mega Millions, by contrast, has been rolling since its last win and sits at $645 million for Tuesday’s draw.

About Us

NumberBuzz USA — the numbers America checks every day.

NumberBuzz USA is a daily-check hub built for one simple habit: the numbers millions of Americans look up every single morning, gathered on one fast, readable page. Instead of opening a dozen different sites, you can check everything here in under a minute.

What you will find here

  • Lottery results — the latest Powerball and Mega Millions winning numbers, the next jackpots, live draw countdowns, hot & cold number statistics, ticket checkers and a jackpot tax calculator.
  • Precious metals — indicative gold and silver spot prices per troy ounce.
  • Gas prices — the AAA national average plus regular gasoline averages for all 50 states.
  • Market numbers — the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq closes, Bitcoin and Ethereum prices, and average US mortgage rates.
  • Deals of the day — standout discounts checked each morning.
  • Weather & sports — tomorrow’s forecast highs for major US cities and last night’s NBA and NHL finals.
  • USA Jobs Today — around 20 fresh job openings across warehouse, driving, healthcare, customer service, remote and federal work.
  • Daily fun — today’s Wordle answer (hidden behind hints, so no accidental spoilers) and a daily horoscope for all 12 signs.

Who runs NumberBuzz USA

NumberBuzz USA is owned and operated by Shahiryar Munir, an independent publisher. The site is a small, independent project — not a news corporation and not affiliated with Powerball, Mega Millions, AAA, or any lottery, employer or retailer mentioned on the page.

How the page is updated

The page is refreshed every morning with a new dated snapshot. Every figure carries its date, and the numbers are compiled from publicly available sources — official lottery results, AAA fuel data, market reports and public job boards — and cross-checked at build time before publishing. Because this is a snapshot rather than a live feed, prices and jackpots can move after publication; the date printed at the top of the page always tells you exactly how fresh the information is.

Our promise is simple: real numbers, clear dates, no invented figures — and if you ever spot something that looks wrong, please tell us via the Contact page so we can fix it in the next refresh.

How to Check Your Powerball Ticket — and What to Do If You Win

Guide · NumberBuzz USA

Checking a Powerball ticket sounds simple, yet every year prizes go unclaimed because someone misread a number, forgot the Powerball itself can win a prize on its own, or threw a ticket away too early. Here is the careful way to check — and the calm, correct steps to take if you win.

Step 1: Check the draw date first

Powerball draws are held every Monday, Wednesday and Saturday at 10:59 p.m. Eastern Time. Your ticket is only valid for the draw date printed on it (unless you bought a multi-draw ticket). Compare your numbers against the result for that exact date — on NumberBuzz, the draw date is always printed next to the game name.

Step 2: Match the five white balls — order does not matter

Your five main numbers (1–69) can match the five white balls in any order. Count your matches slowly, one number at a time. Then check the red Powerball (1–26) separately. Remember: matching the red Powerball alone already wins a $4 prize, and combinations pay at every level — 3 white balls pays $7, 4 white balls pays $100, 4 plus the Powerball pays $50,000, 5 white balls pays $1 million, and all five plus the Powerball wins the jackpot. If you added Power Play, most non-jackpot prizes are multiplied.

Step 3: Double-check before you celebrate — or bin it

Use the ticket checker on our Powerball card, then verify the result a second time against the official Powerball or state lottery listing. Our results are unofficial, and the official source is the only one that counts for a claim. Keep the ticket until you have done both checks.

If you win: the first 24 hours

Sign the back of the ticket immediately — an unsigned winning ticket can be claimed by whoever holds it. Photograph both sides and store the original somewhere safe. For small prizes, your retailer can usually pay you on the spot. For large prizes, stay quiet, take your time, and speak to a lawyer and a financial adviser before claiming; most states give you 180 days to a year. Finally, decide between the lump-sum cash option and the 30-year annuity with real advice — our jackpot tax calculator can give you a rough first estimate of what each choice means after federal and state tax.

Play responsibly. You must be 18+ (21+ in some states) to play.

Powerball vs Mega Millions: Draw Days, Odds and Jackpots Explained

Guide · NumberBuzz USA

They sit side by side in every gas station in America — Powerball costs $2 a play and Mega Millions costs $5 a play (since April 2025) — and both regularly offer jackpots in the hundreds of millions. So what is actually different between Powerball and Mega Millions? Quite a lot — and the differences are worth knowing before you choose.

Draw days and times

Powerball draws three times a week — Monday, Wednesday and Saturday at 10:59 p.m. Eastern. Mega Millions draws twice a week — Tuesday and Friday at 11:00 p.m. Eastern. Together they cover six nights a week, which is why NumberBuzz lists both: there is almost always a big draw tonight or tomorrow night. In our current snapshot, for example, Powerball plays Monday, November 23 at $20 million, while Mega Millions plays Tuesday, November 24 at $645 million.

The number pools

Powerball asks you to pick 5 numbers from 1–69 plus a red Powerball from 1–26. Mega Millions asks for 5 numbers from 1–70 plus a gold Mega Ball from 1–24. The pools look similar, but the slightly larger Mega Millions white-ball pool makes its jackpot a touch harder to hit.

The odds

The jackpot odds are 1 in 292.2 million for Powerball and 1 in 290.5 million for Mega Millions — close enough that neither game is meaningfully “easier” at the top. Where they differ more is the smaller prizes: both games pay $4 for matching only the bonus ball, $1 million for matching all five main numbers, and a ladder of prizes in between. Your overall chance of winning any prize is roughly 1 in 24 in Powerball and 1 in 23 in Mega Millions.

Jackpots and rollovers

Both jackpots grow (“roll over”) whenever nobody matches all six numbers, and both reset after a win. That is why the two jackpots on this page can look wildly different: Powerball reset after its $847 million win in New Jersey on November 4, while Mega Millions has been rolling ever since its last win. Both games pay the jackpot as a 30-year annuity or a smaller lump-sum cash option, and both offer multiplier add-ons (Power Play and the Mega Millions multiplier) that boost non-jackpot prizes.

Which should you play?

Honestly: whichever jackpot is bigger, whichever draw is tonight — or the one whose numbers you simply like. Statistically the games are near-identical, and every combination in both games has exactly the same chance as every other. Play for fun, spend only what you can afford to lose, and always verify results with the official lottery.

Why Gas Prices Change Every Day — and How to Find the Cheapest Fuel Near You

Guide · NumberBuzz USA

You filled up on Monday at one price and drove past the same station on Thursday to find a different one. Gas prices feel random, but they follow a logic — and once you see it, the numbers on our 50-state table start to make sense. On November 19, for example, regular averaged $3.72 nationally, yet North Carolina drivers paid $3.06 while Hawaii paid $5.60.

1. Crude oil is the biggest ingredient

Roughly half the price of a gallon of gasoline is the price of crude oil, which trades on world markets every second. Wars, storms, OPEC decisions and global demand all move crude — and pump prices follow within days.

2. Refineries and seasons

Crude has to be refined, and refinery maintenance, outages or hurricanes on the Gulf Coast can squeeze supply overnight. Twice a year the blend itself changes: cleaner summer-blend fuel costs more to make, which is one reason prices often climb in spring.

3. Taxes and distance explain the state gaps

Every state adds its own fuel tax on top of the federal 18.4¢, and states far from refineries and pipelines — Hawaii, California, the Pacific Northwest — pay more for transport and stricter fuel rules. That is why the cheapest states in our table cluster in the South and Midwest, near Gulf Coast refineries, while the priciest sit on the coasts.

4. Demand moves the daily number

Holiday weekends, summer road trips and even a Friday payday push demand up; a quiet winter week pulls it down. Stations also price against the station across the street, which is why two blocks can mean a 30-cent difference.

How to find the cheapest fuel near you

Check the national and state averages on this page first, so you know what “fair” looks like today. Fill up early in the week — prices often rise toward the weekend. Avoid motorway and airport stations, where convenience is priced in; warehouse clubs and busy supermarket stations are usually cheapest. Keep tyres properly inflated and clear heavy junk out of the trunk — both quietly improve mileage. And when prices are falling, as they are this week (down from $3.75 yesterday to $3.72), there is no rush: waiting a day can genuinely save you money.

State averages shown on NumberBuzz come from AAA’s national survey; your local price will differ — sometimes by a lot.
